title: Chemical Bonding
description: How atoms join together — ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding, giant structures, simple molecules, and explaining properties through bonding.

notes.heading: Why Do Atoms Bond? The Octet Rule
notes.body: Atoms bond to achieve a stable electron configuration — a full outer shell of electrons (usually 8, or 2 for hydrogen and lithium). This is the octet rule. Noble gases already have full outer shells, which is why they are unreactive. All other elements gain, lose, or share electrons to become like a noble gas. There are three main types of bonding: ionic (metal + non-metal, electrons transferred), covalent (non-metal + non-metal, electrons shared), and metallic (metal + metal, electrons delocalised). The type of bonding determines the properties of a substance — melting point, electrical conductivity, solubility, and strength. A useful way to predict bond type: if the elements are far apart on the periodic table (metal + non-metal) → ionic; close together (both non-metals) → covalent; both metals → metallic.

illustration.alt: Diagram comparing an atom with an incomplete outer shell to a noble gas with a full outer shell, and summarising ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding.
illustration.caption: Atoms bond to gain a full outer shell like a noble gas. The three main bonding types are ionic, covalent, and metallic.

notes.heading: Ionic Bonding
notes.body: Ionic bonding occurs when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal. The metal loses electrons → positive ion (cation). The non-metal gains electrons → negative ion (anion). The oppositely charged ions attract each other by strong electrostatic forces — this is the ionic bond. Example: sodium chloride (NaCl). Na (2,8,1) loses 1 electron → Na⁺ (2,8). Cl (2,8,7) gains 1 electron → Cl⁻ (2,8,8). The ions form a giant ionic lattice — a regular, repeating 3D arrangement. Each Na⁺ is surrounded by 6 Cl⁻ and vice versa. Properties of ionic compounds: high melting/boiling points (strong electrostatic forces throughout the lattice require lots of energy to break), do NOT conduct electricity when solid (ions are fixed in place), but DO conduct when molten or dissolved in water (ions are free to move), often soluble in water, brittle (when a layer shifts, like charges align and repel — the crystal shatters). Formula of ionic compounds: the total positive charge must equal total negative charge. Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ → MgCl₂. Al³⁺ + 3O²⁻ → Al₂O₃. Common polyatomic ions: OH⁻ (hydroxide), SO₄²⁻ (sulfate), NO₃⁻ (nitrate), CO₃²⁻ (carbonate), NH₄⁺ (ammonium).

illustration.alt: Sodium transferring an electron to chlorine to form Na+ and Cl- ions, which then pack into a giant ionic lattice.
illustration.caption: Electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal creates ions that are held together by electrostatic attraction in a giant lattice.

notes.heading: Covalent Bonding — Simple Molecules
notes.body: Covalent bonding occurs between non-metal atoms, which share pairs of electrons to achieve full outer shells. Each shared pair = one covalent bond. A single bond is one shared pair (e.g., H-H, Cl-Cl); a double bond is two shared pairs (e.g., O=O); a triple bond is three shared pairs (e.g., N≡N). Simple molecular substances (like H₂O, CO₂, O₂, CH₄) consist of small, discrete molecules held together by strong covalent bonds WITHIN each molecule, but only weak intermolecular forces BETWEEN molecules. This explains their properties: low melting/boiling points (little energy needed to overcome weak intermolecular forces — the covalent bonds themselves do NOT break), do NOT conduct electricity (no ions or free electrons), often gases or liquids at room temperature. As molecules get larger, intermolecular forces get stronger, so boiling points increase (e.g., F₂ and Cl₂ are gases; Br₂ is a liquid; I₂ is a solid — all halogens with increasing molecular size). Drawing dot-and-cross diagrams: show only outer shell electrons, use different symbols (dots/crosses) for different elements, pair up the shared electrons. Examples: H₂O — oxygen shares one pair with each H; CO₂ — carbon shares two pairs with each O (double bonds); CH₄ — carbon shares one pair with each of 4 H atoms.

illustration.alt: Dot-and-cross diagrams for water and methane molecules, showing shared electron pairs and weak intermolecular forces.
illustration.caption: In simple molecular substances, atoms share electron pairs within molecules, but only weak forces act between molecules.

notes.heading: Giant Covalent Structures (Macromolecules)
notes.body: Some covalent substances form giant structures where all atoms are connected by covalent bonds in a continuous network — there are no separate molecules. Key examples: (1) Diamond — each carbon atom bonded covalently to 4 other carbon atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement. Properties: extremely hard (hardest natural substance), very high melting point (~3550°C), does NOT conduct electricity (all electrons fixed in bonds), used for cutting tools and jewellery. (2) Graphite — each carbon bonded to only 3 others in flat hexagonal layers. The 4th outer electron from each carbon is delocalised between the layers. Properties: soft and slippery (layers slide over each other — used as lubricant and pencil 'lead'), high melting point, CONDUCTS electricity (delocalised electrons can move along layers). (3) Silicon dioxide (SiO₂, silica/sand) — similar structure to diamond: each Si bonded to 4 O atoms, each O bonded to 2 Si atoms. Properties: hard, very high melting point, does not conduct. Key comparison: diamond vs graphite — both are pure carbon, but their different structures give them completely different properties. This is allotropy — same element, different structural arrangement.

illustration.alt: Diamond's tetrahedral 3D network compared to graphite's layered hexagonal structure with delocalised electrons.
illustration.caption: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, but their different giant covalent structures give them very different properties.

notes.heading: Metallic Bonding
notes.body: In metals, the outer electrons are delocalised — they are not attached to any specific atom but move freely throughout the metal structure. The metal exists as a regular lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons. The electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the sea of electrons holds the metal together — this is the metallic bond. Properties explained by this model: (1) High melting/boiling points (strong attraction between ions and electrons). (2) Good electrical conductivity (delocalised electrons can flow when a voltage is applied). (3) Good thermal conductivity (electrons transfer kinetic energy rapidly). (4) Malleable and ductile (layers of ions can slide past each other — the sea of electrons moves with them and continues holding the structure together, unlike ionic solids which shatter). (5) Shiny/lustrous (delocalised electrons reflect light). The strength of metallic bonding depends on: the number of delocalised electrons per atom (more electrons = stronger bond → higher melting point) and the size of the ion (smaller ions = closer packing = stronger). This explains why Group 1 metals are soft with low melting points (only 1 delocalised electron per atom), while transition metals are hard with high melting points (many delocalised electrons).

illustration.alt: Positive metal ions arranged in a lattice, surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.
illustration.caption: Metallic bonding is the attraction between positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons that move freely around them.

notes.heading: Comparing Bonding Types — Properties Summary
notes.body: A systematic comparison: Ionic compounds — high MP/BP, conduct when molten/aqueous (ions mobile), brittle, often soluble in water. Simple molecular (covalent) — low MP/BP, never conduct, often gases/liquids at RT, insoluble in water (some exceptions like sugar). Giant covalent — very high MP/BP, do NOT conduct (except graphite), hard, insoluble. Metallic — high MP/BP (variable), ALWAYS conduct as solids, malleable/ductile, insoluble. Key test questions: Why does NaCl conduct when molten but not solid? Ions fixed in lattice → can't move; molten → ions free to move and carry charge. Why is diamond hard but graphite soft? Diamond: 3D tetrahedral network of strong covalent bonds. Graphite: strong covalent bonds within layers, but weak forces BETWEEN layers → layers slide. Why do metals conduct as solids but ionic compounds don't? Metals: delocalised electrons always free. Ionic: ions fixed until molten/dissolved.

illustration.alt: A summary table comparing ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent, and metallic substances by properties.
illustration.caption: Use this comparison table to predict melting point, conductivity, solubility, and other properties from bonding type.

notes.heading: Naming Compounds and Writing Formulae
notes.body: Rules for naming: (1) Metal + non-metal → name ends in '-ide' (sodium chloride, magnesium oxide, iron sulfide). Exception: if oxygen → '-ide' (oxide, not 'oxygenide'). (2) Compound containing oxygen + another non-metal → name ends in '-ate' (copper sulfate CuSO₄, calcium carbonate CaCO₃, potassium nitrate KNO₃). Exception: hydroxide OH⁻. (3) Two non-metals → use prefixes: mono- (1, often omitted for first element), di- (2), tri- (3), tetra- (4). CO₂ = carbon dioxide, PCl₅ = phosphorus pentachloride. Writing formulae using valency (swap-and-drop method): Write symbols, write valencies (charge numbers) above, swap down as subscripts, cancel if needed. Ca²⁺ + Cl⁻ → CaCl₂. Al³⁺ + O²⁻ → Al₂O₃. For covalent compounds, use the prefixes from the name: carbon dioxide = 1 carbon + 2 oxygen = CO₂. State symbols in equations: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous (dissolved in water).

illustration.alt: Naming rules for ionic and covalent compounds, plus the swap-and-drop method for writing formulae with examples.
illustration.caption: Swap the charge numbers down as subscripts to write ionic formulae; use prefixes for two-non-metal compounds.

flashcards.definition: Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal.
flashcards.example: Na⁺Cl⁻ — Na lost 1 electron, Cl gained 1 electron. Giant ionic lattice.

flashcards.definition: A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms. Single bond = 1 pair; double = 2 pairs; triple = 3 pairs.
flashcards.example: H₂O — O shares one pair with each H. CO₂ — C shares two pairs with each O (O=C=O).

flashcards.definition: Electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a 'sea' of delocalised outer electrons.
flashcards.example: Copper wire conducts electricity because delocalised electrons flow freely through the metal lattice.

flashcards.definition: A regular, repeating 3D arrangement of oppositely charged ions. Strong electrostatic forces throughout → high melting point.
flashcards.example: In NaCl, each Na⁺ is surrounded by 6 Cl⁻ ions and vice versa.

flashcards.definition: A substance made of small discrete molecules with strong covalent bonds within molecules but weak forces between them → low MP/BP.
flashcards.example: O₂, H₂O, CO₂, CH₄ — all gases at room temperature. I₂ is a solid (larger molecule, stronger intermolecular forces).

flashcards.definition: Pure carbon — each C atom covalently bonded to 4 others in a tetrahedral 3D network. Extremely hard, very high MP, does NOT conduct electricity.
flashcards.example: Diamond is used for cutting tools and jewellery — the hardest natural material.

flashcards.definition: Pure carbon — each C bonded to 3 others in hexagonal layers. Delocalised electrons between layers. Soft/slippery, conducts electricity.
flashcards.example: Graphite 'lead' in pencils — layers slide off onto paper. Also used as electrodes.

flashcards.definition: Electrons not attached to any specific atom or bond — free to move throughout the structure. Present in metals and graphite.
flashcards.example: Delocalised electrons enable metals to conduct electricity and heat.

flashcards.definition: Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state. Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.
flashcards.example: Both diamond and graphite are 100% carbon, but their different bonding arrangements give completely different properties.

flashcards.definition: A charged particle composed of two or more atoms covalently bonded together. Acts as a single unit in ionic compounds.
Weak attractive forces BETWEEN molecules in simple molecular substances. Easily overcome → low melting and boiling points.
flashcards.example: Boiling water overcomes intermolecular forces between H₂O molecules — the covalent O-H bonds inside each molecule do NOT break.

flashcards.definition: The force of attraction between oppositely charged particles. The basis of ionic bonding (between ions) and metallic bonding (ions to electrons).
flashcards.example: The strong electrostatic forces throughout an ionic lattice require high temperatures to overcome.

questions.stem: A bond forms between a metal (Na) and a non-metal (Cl). What type of bond is this?
choices: Ionic bond — electron transfer from metal to non-metal
questions.explanation: Metal + non-metal = ionic bond. Na loses 1e⁻ → Na⁺; Cl gains 1e⁻ → Cl⁻. Opposite ions attract.

questions.stem: What type of bonding is present in a water molecule (H₂O)?
choices: Covalent — H and O are both non-metals, they share electrons
questions.explanation: Non-metal + non-metal = covalent. O shares one pair of electrons with each H atom.

questions.stem: Why can metals conduct electricity as solids?
choices: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the metal lattice when a voltage is applied
questions.explanation: Metals have a 'sea' of delocalised electrons not attached to any specific atom. These free electrons flow as an electric current.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride (NaCl) does NOT conduct electricity as a solid but DOES when molten. Why?
choices: Solid NaCl has no charged particles
In the solid, ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move; when molten, ions are free to move and carry charge
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds conduct only when ions are mobile. In solids, ions vibrate in fixed positions. Melting frees them to move towards electrodes.

questions.stem: Both diamond and graphite are pure carbon. Why is diamond hard but graphite soft?
choices: Diamond: 3D tetrahedral network of strong covalent bonds in all directions. Graphite: strong bonds within layers, weak forces BETWEEN layers → layers slide
Graphite has impurities that make it soft
questions.explanation: Structure determines properties. Diamond's continuous 3D covalent network makes it hard. Graphite's layered structure (weak interlayer forces) allows layers to slide.

questions.stem: What is the formula of aluminium oxide? (Al³⁺, O²⁻)
questions.explanation: Swap-and-drop: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ → Al₂O₃. Total positive charge = 2×3+ = 6+; total negative = 3×2− = 6−. Charges balance.

questions.stem: Why do simple molecular substances like CO₂ have low boiling points?
choices: The covalent bonds in CO₂ are weak
Only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome — the covalent bonds within molecules do NOT break
questions.explanation: Boiling a simple molecular substance overcomes weak intermolecular forces between molecules. The strong covalent bonds within each molecule remain intact.

questions.stem: Which of these substances conducts electricity as a solid?
questions.explanation: Copper is a metal — it has delocalised electrons that conduct. NaCl needs to be molten; diamond has no free electrons; water is molecular.

questions.stem: Magnesium oxide (MgO) has a very high melting point (~2852°C). Why?
choices: MgO has a giant ionic lattice — Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are held by strong electrostatic forces throughout. MgO has 2+/2− ions (stronger than 1+/1− in NaCl)
questions.explanation: MgO is ionic with doubly charged ions (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻). The electrostatic attraction is stronger than in NaCl (Na⁺/Cl⁻), so the melting point is much higher.

questions.stem: In a dot-and-cross diagram of methane (CH₄), how many shared pairs of electrons are there?
choices: 4 — carbon shares one pair with each of the 4 hydrogen atoms
questions.explanation: CH₄ has 4 single covalent bonds. Each H shares 1 electron pair with the central C atom. C achieves a full outer shell (8 electrons total from sharing).

questions.stem: Why are metals malleable (can be hammered into shape) but ionic compounds are brittle?
choices: In metals, layers of ions slide while the sea of electrons adapts. In ionic lattices, shifting layers brings like charges together → repulsion → shattering
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding's delocalised electrons allow layers to slide past each other without breaking bonds. Ionic lattices shatter because shifting aligns like-charged ions (++ or −−), causing repulsion.

questions.stem: Name the compound N₂O₄ using prefixes.
questions.explanation: Two non-metals → use prefixes: di- (2 N) + tetr- (4 O) + -oxide = dinitrogen tetroxide. (Drop the 'a' in tetra before oxide.)

questions.stem: Which type of bonding explains why transition metals have higher melting points than Group 1 metals?
choices: Transition metals have more delocalised electrons per atom → stronger metallic bonding → higher melting points
Transition metals form giant covalent structures
questions.explanation: More delocalised electrons per atom means a stronger electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the electron sea → more energy required to melt.

questions.stem: Graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. Why?
choices: Graphite has delocalised electrons (4th outer electron from each C) between layers that can move; in diamond, all 4 outer electrons are fixed in covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Carbon has 4 outer electrons. In diamond, all 4 form covalent bonds — no free electrons. In graphite, only 3 form bonds; the 4th is delocalised between layers → can conduct.

questions.stem: Calcium nitrate contains Ca²⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions. What is its formula?
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻ to balance: 1 × (+2) + 2 × (−1) = 0. Brackets show two nitrate ions. Formula = Ca(NO₃)₂.
